claim: Unusual 3→3 cross-links formed by L,D-transpeptidases were first detected in Escherichia coli more than four decades ago.
source: Unusual 3→3 cross-links formed by L,D-transpeptidases were first detected in Escherichia coli more than four decades ago, however no phenotype has previously been associated with their synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to historical work (Schwarz et al., 1969) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: No phenotype has previously been associated with the synthesis of 3→3 cross-links in E. coli.
source: Unusual 3→3 cross-links formed by L,D-transpeptidases were first detected in Escherichia coli more than four decades ago, however no phenotype has previously been associated with their synthesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior findings in the literature.

claim: Production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB in combination with elevated synthesis of the (p)ppGpp alarmone by RelA leads to full bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs.
source: Here we show that production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB in combination with elevated synthesis of the (p)ppGpp alarmone by RelA lead to full bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs and to broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including genetic analyses, peptidoglycan structure analysis, and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

claim: Production of YcbB in combination with elevated (p)ppGpp synthesis leads to broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
source: Here we show that production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB in combination with elevated synthesis of the (p)ppGpp alarmone by RelA lead to full bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs and to broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is supported by disk diffusion assays and MIC determinations shown in Tables 1 and 5.

claim: Production of YcbB is sufficient to switch the role of (p)ppGpp from antibiotic tolerance to high-level β-lactam resistance.
source: Production of YcbB was therefore sufficient to switch the role of (p)ppGpp from antibiotic tolerance to high-level β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that YcbB production combined with (p)ppGpp synthesis confers resistance rather than tolerance.

claim: Peptidoglycan polymerization in the YcbB-mediated resistance mechanism relies on the glycosyltransferase activity of class A PBP1b.
source: This observation identifies a new mode of peptidoglycan polymerization in E. coli that relies on an unexpectedly small number of enzyme activities comprising the glycosyltransferase activity of class A PBP1b and the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of DacA in addition to the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB.
evidence: This is supported by genetic deletion studies and complementation experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: Peptidoglycan polymerization in the YcbB-mediated resistance mechanism relies on the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of DacA (PBP5).
source: This observation identifies a new mode of peptidoglycan polymerization in E. coli that relies on an unexpectedly small number of enzyme activities comprising the glycosyltransferase activity of class A PBP1b and the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of DacA in addition to the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB.
evidence: This is supported by genetic deletion studies showing that dacA is essential for YcbB-mediated resistance (Table 2).

claim: Peptidoglycan is a giant macromolecule with a molecular weight of 10^9 to 10^10 Da.
source: Peptidoglycan, the major component of bacterial cell walls, is a giant (109 to 1010 Da) net-like macromolecule composed of glycan strands cross-linked by short peptides (Turner et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2014.

claim: Peptidoglycan is composed of glycan strands cross-linked by short peptides.
source: Peptidoglycan, the major component of bacterial cell walls, is a giant (109 to 1010 Da) net-like macromolecule composed of glycan strands cross-linked by short peptides (Turner et al., 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Glycan strands in peptidoglycan are polymerized by glycosyltransferases.
source: The glycan strands are polymerized by glycosyltransferases and the cross-links are formed by D,D-transpeptidases.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cross-links in peptidoglycan are formed by D,D-transpeptidases.
source: The glycan strands are polymerized by glycosyltransferases and the cross-links are formed by D,D-transpeptidases.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: D,D-transpeptidases cleave the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 peptide bond of an acyl donor stem.
source: The latter enzymes cleave the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 peptide bond of an acyl donor stem and link the carbonyl of D-Ala4 to the side chain amine of diaminopimelic acid (DAP) of the acceptor stem, thereby generating D-Ala4→DAP3 cross-links (Figure 1A) (Pratt, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pratt, 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: D,D-transpeptidases link the carbonyl of D-Ala4 to the side chain amine of diaminopimelic acid (DAP) of the acceptor stem, generating D-Ala4→DAP3 cross-links.
source: The latter enzymes cleave the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 peptide bond of an acyl donor stem and link the carbonyl of D-Ala4 to the side chain amine of diaminopimelic acid (DAP) of the acceptor stem, thereby generating D-Ala4→DAP3 cross-links (Figure 1A) (Pratt, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pratt, 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: β-lactam antibiotics mimic the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 termination of peptidoglycan precursors.
source: β-lactam antibiotics mimic the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 termination of peptidoglycan precursors and inactivate the D,D-transpeptidases by acting as suicide substrates (Tipper and Strominger, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tipper and Strominger, 1965 and is established knowledge.

claim: β-lactam antibiotics inactivate D,D-transpeptidases by acting as suicide substrates.
source: β-lactam antibiotics mimic the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 termination of peptidoglycan precursors and inactivate the D,D-transpeptidases by acting as suicide substrates (Tipper and Strominger, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tipper and Strominger, 1965 and is established knowledge.

claim: D,D-transpeptidases belong to a diverse family of proteins commonly referred to as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
source: The D,D-transpeptidases belong to a diverse family of proteins, commonly referred to as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), that fall into three main classes (Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sauvage et al., 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: PBPs fall into three main classes.
source: The D,D-transpeptidases belong to a diverse family of proteins, commonly referred to as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), that fall into three main classes (Sauvage et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sauvage et al., 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: Class A PBPs (PBP1a, 1b, and 1c) combine glycosyltransferase and D,D-transpeptidase modules.
source: Class A PBPs (PBP1a, 1b, and 1c) combine glycosyltransferase and D,D-transpeptidase modules.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class B PBPs (PBP2 and 3) are composed of a nonenzymatic morphogenesis module fused to a D,D-transpeptidase module.
source: Class B PBPs (PBP2 and 3) are composed of a nonenzymatic morphogenesis module fused to a D,D-transpeptidase module.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class C PBPs (PBP4, 4b, 5, 6, 6b, 7, and AmpH) are monofunctional enzymes with D,D-carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities.
source: Class C PBPs (PBP4, 4b, 5, 6, 6b, 7, and AmpH) are monofunctional enzymes with D,D-carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities that hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 bond of pentapeptide stems and the D-Ala4→DAP3 bond of cross-linked peptidoglycan, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class C PBPs hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 bond of pentapeptide stems.
source: Class C PBPs (PBP4, 4b, 5, 6, 6b, 7, and AmpH) are monofunctional enzymes with D,D-carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities that hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 bond of pentapeptide stems and the D-Ala4→DAP3 bond of cross-linked peptidoglycan, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Class C PBPs hydrolyze the D-Ala4→DAP3 bond of cross-linked peptidoglycan.
source: Class C PBPs (PBP4, 4b, 5, 6, 6b, 7, and AmpH) are monofunctional enzymes with D,D-carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities that hydrolyze the D-Ala4-D-Ala5 bond of pentapeptide stems and the D-Ala4→DAP3 bond of cross-linked peptidoglycan, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Peptidoglycan polymerization involves two complexes: the divisome and the elongasome.
source: Peptidoglycan polymerization involves two complexes (Figure 1B), the divisome and the elongasome, responsible for septum formation and lateral cell-wall elongation, respectively (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: The divisome is responsible for septum formation.
source: Peptidoglycan polymerization involves two complexes (Figure 1B), the divisome and the elongasome, responsible for septum formation and lateral cell-wall elongation, respectively (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: The elongasome is responsible for lateral cell-wall elongation.
source: Peptidoglycan polymerization involves two complexes (Figure 1B), the divisome and the elongasome, responsible for septum formation and lateral cell-wall elongation, respectively (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008 and is established knowledge.

claim: The divisome and elongasome complexes include all the biosynthetic and hydrolytic enzymes required for the incorporation of new subunits into the expanding peptidoglycan net.
source: These complexes include all the biosynthetic and hydrolytic enzymes required for the incorporation of new subunits into the expanding peptidoglycan net, as well as cytoskeletal proteins, MreB and FtsZ, acting as guiding devices.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The divisome and elongasome complexes include cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ that act as guiding devices.
source: These complexes include all the biosynthetic and hydrolytic enzymes required for the incorporation of new subunits into the expanding peptidoglycan net, as well as cytoskeletal proteins, MreB and FtsZ, acting as guiding devices.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Unusual cross-links connecting two DAP residues were detected in E. coli as early as 1969.
source: Unusual cross-links connecting two DAP residues were detected in E. coli as early as 1969, however the enzymes responsible for their formation at that time were unknown (Schwarz et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 1969.

claim: The enzymes responsible for DAP3→DAP3 cross-link formation were unknown in 1969.
source: Unusual cross-links connecting two DAP residues were detected in E. coli as early as 1969, however the enzymes responsible for their formation at that time were unknown (Schwarz et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 1969.

claim: DAP3→DAP3 cross-links account for 3% of the cross-links present in peptidoglycan extracted from bacteria in the exponential phase of growth.
source: These DAP3→DAP3 cross-links account for 3% and 10% of the cross-links present in the peptidoglycan extracted from bacteria in the exponential and stationary phases of growth, respectively (Schwarz et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 1969.

claim: DAP3→DAP3 cross-links account for 10% of the cross-links present in peptidoglycan extracted from bacteria in the stationary phase of growth.
source: These DAP3→DAP3 cross-links account for 3% and 10% of the cross-links present in the peptidoglycan extracted from bacteria in the exponential and stationary phases of growth, respectively (Schwarz et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz et al., 1969.

claim: L,D-transpeptidases responsible for the formation of 3→3 cross-links in various bacterial species have been identified.
source: More recently, we have identified the L,D-transpeptidases (Ldt) responsible for the formation of 3→3 cross-links in various bacterial species and shown that these enzymes are structurally unrelated to PBPs (Mainardi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mainardi et al., 2008.

claim: L,D-transpeptidases are structurally unrelated to PBPs.
source: More recently, we have identified the L,D-transpeptidases (Ldt) responsible for the formation of 3→3 cross-links in various bacterial species and shown that these enzymes are structurally unrelated to PBPs (Mainardi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mainardi et al., 2008.

claim: The chromosome of E. coli encodes five L,D-transpeptidases with distinct functions.
source: Gene deletion and complementation analyses have indicated that the chromosome of E. coli encodes five L,D-transpeptidases with distinct functions.
evidence: This is supported by gene deletion and complementation analyses cited in the manuscript.

claim: Two L,D-transpeptidase paralogues (YcbB and YnhG) form the DAP3→DAP3 peptidoglycan cross-links.
source: Two paralogues form the DAP3→DAP3 peptidoglycan cross-links (YcbB and YnhG) (Magnet et al., 2008), whereas the three remaining paralogues anchor the Braun lipoprotein to peptidoglycan (YbiS, ErfK, and YcfS) (Magnet et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Magnet et al., 2008.

claim: Three L,D-transpeptidase paralogues (YbiS, ErfK, and YcfS) anchor the Braun lipoprotein to peptidoglycan.
source: Two paralogues form the DAP3→DAP3 peptidoglycan cross-links (YcbB and YnhG) (Magnet et al., 2008), whereas the three remaining paralogues anchor the Braun lipoprotein to peptidoglycan (YbiS, ErfK, and YcfS) (Magnet et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Magnet et al., 2007.

claim: The L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB is able to replace the D,D-transpeptidase activity of all five class A and B PBPs of E. coli.
source: Here we show that the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB, but not that of YnhG, is able to replace the D,D-transpeptidase activity of all five class A and B PBPs of E. coli, leading to β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing resistance in the presence of YcbB and inhibitors of class A and B PBPs.

claim: The L,D-transpeptidase activity of YnhG is not able to replace the D,D-transpeptidase activity of all five class A and B PBPs of E. coli.
source: Here we show that the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB, but not that of YnhG, is able to replace the D,D-transpeptidase activity of all five class A and B PBPs of E. coli, leading to β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that expression of ynhG did not confer ampicillin resistance.

claim: β-lactams of the penam and cephem classes effectively inactivate D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the PBP family.
source: β-lactams of the penam and cephem classes, such as ampicillin and ceftriaxone, respectively, effectively inactivate D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the PBP family.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: L,D-transpeptidases are slowly acylated by penam and cephem β-lactams.
source: In contrast, L,D-transpeptidases are slowly acylated by these drugs and the resulting acyl-enzymes are unstable (Triboulet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Triboulet et al., 2013.

claim: Acyl-enzymes formed between L,D-transpeptidases and penam/cephem β-lactams are unstable.
source: In contrast, L,D-transpeptidases are slowly acylated by these drugs and the resulting acyl-enzymes are unstable (Triboulet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Triboulet et al., 2013.

claim: Slow acylation combined with acyl-enzyme hydrolysis results in partial L,D-transpeptidase inhibition by penam and cephem β-lactams.
source: This accounts for L,D-transpeptidase-mediated penam and cephem resistance since slow acylation combined with acyl-enzyme hydrolysis results in partial L,D-transpeptidase inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical properties of L,D-transpeptidases.

claim: Plasmid pJEH11(ycbB) did not confer ampicillin resistance to strain BW25113Δ4 in the absence of IPTG or in media containing low concentrations of IPTG (up to 50 µM).
source: Plasmid pJEH11(ycbB) did not confer ampicillin resistance to this host in the absence of IPTG or in media containing low concentrations of this inducer (up to 50 µM).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of antibiotic susceptibility.

claim: Induction of ycbB expression with IPTG concentrations greater than 50 µM prevented bacterial growth.
source: Induction of ycbB expression with IPTG concentrations greater than 50 µM prevented bacterial growth, indicating that high-level production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB was toxic.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of bacterial growth.

claim: High-level production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB is toxic to E. coli.
source: Induction of ycbB expression with IPTG concentrations greater than 50 µM prevented bacterial growth, indicating that high-level production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB was toxic.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that high IPTG concentrations prevented growth.

claim: Mutant M1 harbors two mutations.
source: Genetic analyses showed that mutant M1 harbors two mutations.
evidence: This is based on genetic sequencing data.

claim: Mutant M1 displays IPTG-inducible resistance to ampicillin and ceftriaxone.
source: Selection for ampicillin resistance (32 µg/ml) in the presence of IPTG (500 µM) yielded mutant M1, which was not inhibited by 500 µM IPTG and displayed IPTG-inducible resistance to ampicillin and ceftriaxone (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by disk diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The plasmid-borne mutation in mutant M1 is located in the lacI gene resulting in an Arg127Leu substitution.
source: Sequencing revealed a mutation located in the vector-born lacI gene resulting in an Arg127Leu substitution in the inducer binding site.
evidence: This is based on DNA sequencing data.

claim: The plasmid-borne lacI mutation abolished YcbB toxicity by decreasing the level of ycbB transcription in inducing conditions.
source: Thus, the plasmid-borne mutation abolished YcbB toxicity by decreasing the level of ycbB transcription in inducing conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the mutation in lacI reduced toxicity.

claim: The toxicity associated with high-level production of YcbB may be linked to the putative membrane anchor of the protein.
source: The toxicity associated with high-level production of YcbB may be linked to the putative membrane anchor of the protein as demonstrated for PBP2 in E. coli (Legaree et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to PBP2, supported by citation to Legaree et al., 2007.

claim: A chromosomal mutation is required for ampicillin resistance in addition to the expression of the plasmid copy of ycbB.
source: These results indicate that a chromosomal mutation is required for ampicillin resistance in addition to the expression of the plasmid copy of ycbB.
evidence: This is based on genetic complementation experiments.

claim: IPTG-inducible expression of ycbB, in combination with the chromosomal mutation, confers broad-spectrum resistance to β-lactams, with the exception of carbapenems.
source: Testing a large panel of β-lactams using the disk diffusion assay indicated that IPTG-inducible expression of ycbB, in combination with the chromosomal mutation, confers broad-spectrum resistance to β-lactams, with the exception of carbapenems (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by disk diffusion assay data shown in Table 1.

claim: In the presence of ampicillin, all cross-links in mutant M1 peptidoglycan were of the 3→3 type.
source: In the presence of ampicillin, the D,D-transpeptidase activity of the PBPs was inhibited, and all cross-links were of the 3→3 type.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of peptidoglycan fragments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: YcbB is sufficient for peptidoglycan cross-linking in the absence of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of the PBPs.
source: These results indicate that YcbB is sufficient for peptidoglycan cross-linking in the absence of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of the PBPs.
evidence: This is based on the observation that all cross-links were 3→3 type in the presence of ampicillin.

claim: Incubation of YcbB with a disaccharide-tetrapeptide resulted in the formation of a peptidoglycan dimer containing a DAP3→DAP3 cross-link.
source: Incubation of YcbB with a disaccharide-tetrapeptide prepared from the peptidoglycan of E. coli resulted in the formation of a peptidoglycan dimer containing a DAP3→DAP3 cross-link (Figures 5 and 6A).
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6A.

claim: Purified YcbB displays L,D-carboxypeptidase activity.
source: Purified YcbB also displayed L,D-carboxypeptidase activity as the enzyme removed the C-terminal residue (D-Ala4) from the tetrapeptide stem (Figures 5 and 6A).
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme assay data shown in Figures 5 and 6A.

claim: YcbB is a bona fide L,D-transpeptidase.
source: These results confirm that YcbB is a bona fide L,D-transpeptidase, which directly accounts for the synthesis of DAP3→DAP3 cross-links in mutant M1.
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme activity data.

claim: Incubation of YcbB with meropenem and imipenem led to full and irreversible acylation of the protein.
source: Incubation of YcbB with representatives of the β-lactams belonging to the carbapenem class, i.e. meropenem and imipenem, led to full and irreversible acylation of the protein, as detected by mass spectrometry (Figures 6B and 7).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figures 6B and 7.

claim: Adducts resulting from acylation of YcbB by β-lactams of the penam and cephem classes were prone to hydrolysis.
source: In contrast, adducts resulting from acylation of YcbB by β-lactams of the penam and cephem classes were prone to hydrolysis (data no shown), as previously described for Ldtfm from E. faecium (Triboulet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and citation to Triboulet et al., 2013.

claim: The inhibition profile of purified YcbB accounts for broad-spectrum resistance to all β-lactams except carbapenems.
source: Thus, the inhibition profile of purified YcbB accounts for broad-spectrum resistance to all β-lactams except carbapenems (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme inhibition data and susceptibility testing shown in Table 1.

claim: Purified YcbB used as the acyl donor a disaccharide-tetrapeptide ending in D-Ala4, but not a disaccharide-pentapeptide ending in D-Ala4-D-Ala5.
source: Purified YcbB used as the acyl donor a disaccharide-tetrapeptide ending in D-Ala4, but not a disaccharide-pentapeptide ending in D-Ala4-D-Ala5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5 is essential for YcbB-mediated β-lactam resistance.
source: Thus, the D,D-carboxypeptidase PBP5 was essential for YcbB-mediated β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion and complementation experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: Independent deletions of dacB, dacC, and dacD had no impact on the frequency of selection of ceftriaxone-resistant mutants.
source: In contrast, independent deletions of dacB, dacC, and dacD encoding PBP4, PBP6, and PBP6b, respectively, had no impact on the frequency of selection of ceftriaxone-resistant mutants (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: The D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5 is necessary and sufficient to generate the essential tetrapeptide-containing substrate of YcbB.
source: These results indicate that the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5 is necessary and sufficient to generate the essential tetrapeptide-containing substrate of YcbB.
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion and complementation experiments in strain CS801-4 shown in Table 3.

claim: PBP5 is only inhibited by high concentrations of β-lactams.
source: It is of note that PBP5 is only inhibited by high concentrations of β-lactams (Curtis et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Curtis et al., 1979.

claim: PBP1b is an essential partner of YcbB for peptidoglycan polymerization in the presence of β-lactams.
source: Ceftriaxone-resistant mutants were obtained with the mrcA, pbpC, and mgtA mutants, but not with the mrcB mutant, indicating that PBP1b is an essential partner of YcbB for peptidoglycan polymerization in the presence of β-lactams.
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: The glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, but not its D,D-transpeptidase activity, is required for YcbB-mediated β-lactam resistance.
source: Selection of ceftriaxone-resistant mutants was obtained in both cases. Thus, the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, but not its D,D-transpeptidase activity, is required for YcbB-mediated β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is based on experiments with PBP1b S510A mutant shown in Table 2.

claim: The glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b is necessary and sufficient for glycan-chain elongation when YcbB is the only functional cross-linking enzyme.
source: Together, these results indicate that the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b is necessary and sufficient for glycan-chain elongation when YcbB is the only functional cross-linking enzyme.
evidence: This is based on experiments with strain BW25113Δ4GT lacking all glycosyltransferase genes except mrcB.

claim: LpoB is essential for the participation of PBP1b in glycan-chain elongation in the context of peptidoglycan cross-linking by YcbB.
source: As expected, ampicillin-resistant mutants were only obtained with the lpoA mutant (Table 2), indicating that LpoB is essential for the participation of PBP1b in glycan-chain elongation in the context of peptidoglycan cross-linking by YcbB.
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: E. coli produces two class B PBPs, PBP2 and PBP3, which are essential.
source: E. coli produces two class B PBPs, PBP2 and PBP3, which are essential and specifically inhibited by mecillinam (Spratt, 1977; Vinella et al., 1993) and aztreonam (Georgopapadakou et al., 1982), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PBP2 is specifically inhibited by mecillinam.
source: E. coli produces two class B PBPs, PBP2 and PBP3, which are essential and specifically inhibited by mecillinam (Spratt, 1977; Vinella et al., 1993) and aztreonam (Georgopapadakou et al., 1982), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PBP3 is specifically inhibited by aztreonam.
source: E. coli produces two class B PBPs, PBP2 and PBP3, which are essential and specifically inhibited by mecillinam (Spratt, 1977; Vinella et al., 1993) and aztreonam (Georgopapadakou et al., 1982), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutant M1 was resistant to mecillinam and aztreonam in the presence of IPTG.
source: In the presence of IPTG, mutant M1 was resistant to mecillinam and aztreonam, indicating that inhibition of the D,D-transpeptidase module of the class B PBPs did not impair YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance (Table 1 and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on antibiotic susceptibility testing shown in Table 1.

claim: Inhibition of the D,D-transpeptidase module of the class B PBPs did not impair YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance.
source: In the presence of IPTG, mutant M1 was resistant to mecillinam and aztreonam, indicating that inhibition of the D,D-transpeptidase module of the class B PBPs did not impair YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance (Table 1 and data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the resistance to mecillinam and aztreonam.

claim: M1 was resistant to mecillinam in the absence of IPTG.
source: Surprisingly, M1 was resistant to mecillinam in the absence of IPTG.
evidence: This is based on antibiotic susceptibility testing.

claim: Resistance to mecillinam in M1cured was mediated by a chromosomal mutation independently from YcbB production.
source: M1cured was also resistant to mecillinam, indicating that resistance to this antibiotic was mediated by a chromosomal mutation independently from YcbB production (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on antibiotic susceptibility testing of M1cured shown in Table 1.

claim: Acquisition of a mutation conferring mecillinam resistance is necessary and sufficient for YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance.
source: These results indicate that acquisition of a mutation conferring mecillinam resistance is necessary and sufficient for YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance.
evidence: This is based on analysis of independently selected mutants.

claim: Only a portion of the mutations conferring mecillinam resistance enabled YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance.
source: In contrast, only a portion of the mutations conferring mecillinam resistance enabled YcbB-mediated ampicillin resistance.
evidence: This is based on analysis of independently selected mutants showing that 4 of 7 mecillinam-resistant mutants did not display ampicillin resistance.

claim: Mutants M1 to M7 each harbored a single mutation.
source: Whole genome sequencing revealed that mutants M1 to M7 each harbored a single mutation (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 4.

claim: A single mutation is responsible for mecillinam resistance in the absence of YcbB and for YcbB-mediated broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance upon ycbB induction by IPTG.
source: This observation confirms that a single mutation is responsible for mecillinam resistance in the absence of YcbB and for YcbB-mediated broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance upon ycbB induction by IPTG.
evidence: This is inferred from the whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Mutant M1 harbored a 13-bp deletion located in an untranslated region upstream from the isoleucine-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) gene.
source: Mutant M1 harbored a 13-bp deletion located in an untranslated region upstream from the isoleucine-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) gene.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 4.

claim: Mutants M2 to M7 harbored missense mutations in genes encoding ArgRS, ThrRS, GluRS, and AspRS.
source: The remaining mutants (M2 to M7) harbored missense mutations in genes encoding ArgRS, ThrRS, GluRS, and AspRS, with two distinct substitutions for the latter two enzymes.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 4.

claim: The deletion in M1 most probably impairs translation of IleRS since it ends 5 nucleotides upstream from the ATG codon and includes the ribosome binding site.
source: The deletion present in M1 most probably impairs translation of IleRS since it ends 5 nucleotides upstream from the ATG codon and includes the ribosome binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the deletion.

claim: The mutation in M1 impairs aminoacylation of tRNAIle, a defect known to result in activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA in response to ribosomal stalling.
source: Thus, the mutation present in M1 impaired aminoacylation of tRNAIle, a defect known to result in activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA in response to ribosomal stalling, following occupancy of the ribosome acceptor site by uncharged tRNAs (Hauryliuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutation's effect and supported by citation to Hauryliuk et al., 2015.

claim: Missense mutations in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes of mutants M2 to M7 likely result in activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA.
source: The same conclusion is also likely to apply to missense mutations in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes of mutants M2 to M7, although we cannot exclude the possibility that the corresponding amino acid substitutions altered other properties of the proteins.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to M1.

claim: YcbB production and increased (p)ppGpp synthesis are both required for bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs and broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
source: These results indicate that YcbB production and increased (p)ppGpp synthesis are both required for bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of PBPs and broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is based on experiments with inducible expression of YcbB and RelA 1-455 shown in Figure 8.

claim: Production of (p)ppGpp by RelA 1–455 recapitulates the phenotype conferred by mutations in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes of mutants M1 to M7.
source: Production of (p)ppGpp by RelA 1–455 recapitulates the phenotype conferred by mutations in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes of mutants M1 to M7, in agreement with their proposed role in the activation of (p)ppGpp synthesis by RelA in response to binding of uncharged tRNAs to the ribosome acceptor site.
evidence: This is based on experiments with inducible expression of RelA 1-455 shown in Figure 8.

claim: Intense labeling with NADA was detected at mid-cell indicating that YcbB and its tetrapeptide substrate are co-localized in the septum.
source: As shown in Figure 9, intense labeling was detected at mid-cell indicating that YcbB and its tetrapeptide substrate are co-localized in the septum.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Labeling with NADA was inhibited by meropenem, which inactivates YcbB and PBPs.
source: As controls, we also showed that labeling was inhibited by meropenem, which inactivates YcbB and PBPs, but not by ampicillin, which only inactivates PBPs.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Labeling with NADA was not inhibited by ampicillin, which only inactivates PBPs.
source: As controls, we also showed that labeling was inhibited by meropenem, which inactivates YcbB and PBPs, but not by ampicillin, which only inactivates PBPs.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: E. coli can resist β-lactams through bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of high-molecular-weight PBPs.
source: Here we show that E. coli can also resist β-lactams through bypass of the D,D-transpeptidase activity of high-molecular-weight PBPs.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The resistance mechanism required production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB, which was purified and shown to catalyze the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in vitro.
source: The resistance mechanism required production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB, which was purified and shown to catalyze the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in vitro (Figure 6A) and to be inactivated only by carbapenems (Figure 6B), accounting for broad-spectrum resistance to other classes of β-lactams (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YcbB is inactivated only by carbapenems.
source: The resistance mechanism required production of the L,D-transpeptidase YcbB, which was purified and shown to catalyze the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in vitro (Figure 6A) and to be inactivated only by carbapenems (Figure 6B), accounting for broad-spectrum resistance to other classes of β-lactams (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In wild-type strains, lateral expansion of the peptidoglycan network and the formation of the septum involve two protein complexes, the elongasome and the divisome.
source: In wild-type strains, lateral expansion of the peptidoglycan network and the formation of the septum involve two protein complexes, the elongasome and the divisome, respectively, which integrate distinct sets of peptidoglycan polymerases with partially overlapping functions (den Blaauwen et al., 2008) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008.

claim: The L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB is sufficient for peptidoglycan cross-linking in mutant M1.
source: In contrast, the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB is sufficient for peptidoglycan cross-linking in mutant M1.
evidence: This is based on the exclusive detection of DAP3→DAP3 cross-links in the presence of ampicillin.

claim: In wild-type strains, glycan chains are polymerized by either PBP1a or PBP1b.
source: In wild-type strains, glycan chains are polymerized by either PBP1a or PBP1b, although the former is preferentially associated with the elongasome and the latter with the divisome (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008.

claim: PBP1a is preferentially associated with the elongasome.
source: In wild-type strains, glycan chains are polymerized by either PBP1a or PBP1b, although the former is preferentially associated with the elongasome and the latter with the divisome (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008.

claim: PBP1b is preferentially associated with the divisome.
source: In wild-type strains, glycan chains are polymerized by either PBP1a or PBP1b, although the former is preferentially associated with the elongasome and the latter with the divisome (den Blaauwen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to den Blaauwen et al., 2008.

claim: PBP1b, together with its cognate lipoprotein LpoB, are both essential and sufficient for peptidoglycan polymerization in mutant M1 exposed to ampicillin.
source: In contrast, PBP1b, together with its cognate lipoprotein LpoB, are both essential and sufficient for peptidoglycan polymerization in mutant M1 exposed to ampicillin.
evidence: This is based on genetic deletion and complementation experiments.

claim: YcbB activity is preferentially located in the septum.
source: Peptidoglycan labeling with a fluorescent D-amino acid indicated that YcbB activity is preferentially located in the septum, as is its PBP1b partner (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The cross-linking and glycosyltransferase activities of YcbB and PBP1b were sufficient for lateral extension of the peptidoglycan network since bacterial cells retained a rod shape in the presence of ampicillin.
source: The cross-linking and glycosyltransferase activities of YcbB and PBP1b were nonetheless sufficient for lateral extension of the peptidoglycan network since bacterial cells retained a rod shape in the presence of ampicillin.
evidence: This is based on microscopic observation of cell morphology.

claim: The cross-linking activity of high-molecular-weight PBPs is not indispensable to the maintenance of cell shape in E. coli.
source: This observation indicates that the cross-linking activity of high-molecular-weight PBPs is not indispensable to the maintenance of cell shape in E. coli.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells retained rod shape with only YcbB-mediated cross-linking.

claim: A minimum set of enzyme activities necessary and sufficient for peptidoglycan polymerization in the presence of β-lactams comprises the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB, the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, and the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5.
source: Together, our data identified a minimum set of enzyme activities that are necessary and sufficient for peptidoglycan polymerization in the presence of β-lactams (Figure 10). This set comprises the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB, the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, and the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5, which provides the essential tetrapeptide substrate of YcbB.
evidence: This is based on the combined results of genetic deletion and complementation experiments.

claim: LpoB directly stimulates the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b.
source: For example, the fact that LpoB remains essential in the L,D-transpeptidation context indicates that it directly stimulates the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, as indicated in a recent study (Markovski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the essentiality of LpoB and supported by citation to Markovski et al., 2016.

claim: Increased synthesis of the alarmone (p)ppGpp by RelA was required for broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance in addition to YcbB production.
source: In addition to YcbB production, increased synthesis of the alarmone (p)ppGpp by RelA was required for broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance.
evidence: This is based on experiments with inducible expression of RelA 1-455 shown in Figure 8 and Table 5.

claim: PBP2 is not indispensable in E. coli when (p)ppGpp synthesis is increased, leading to mecillinam resistance.
source: Prior analyses also showed that PBP2 is not indispensable in E. coli when (p)ppGpp synthesis is increased, leading to mecillinam resistance (Vinella et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vinella et al., 1992.

claim: Increased (p)ppGpp synthesis regulates growth rate and several different stress responses, including the response to exposure to antibiotics.
source: Aside from mecillinam resistance, increased (p)ppGpp synthesis has also been shown to regulate growth rate and several different stress responses, including the response to exposure to antibiotics (Hauryliuk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hauryliuk et al., 2015.

claim: Tolerance to ampicillin mediated by increased (p)ppGpp synthesis leads to a 1000-fold reduction in bacterial killing.
source: In E. coli, tolerance to ampicillin mediated by increased (p)ppGpp synthesis leads to a 1000-fold reduction in bacterial killing.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cascade triggered by elevated (p)ppGpp involves an increase in the intracellular concentration of polyphosphate via inhibition of the exopolyphosphatase PPX.
source: The cascade triggered by elevated (p)ppGpp involves an increase in the intracellular concentration of polyphosphate via inhibition of the exopolyphosphatase PPX.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Elevated polyphosphate stimulates the protease activity of Lon, which degrades antitoxins, thereby activating the toxins that prevent bacterial killing through inhibition of translation and bacterial growth.
source: In turn, elevated polyphosphate stimulates the protease activity of Lon, which degrades antitoxins, thereby activating the toxins that prevent bacterial killing through inhibition of translation and bacterial growth.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Persistence emerges from stochastic events that render a limited number of bacterial cells transiently tolerant to multiple families of antibiotics.
source: Persistence emerges from stochastic events that render a limited number of bacterial cells transiently tolerant to multiple families of antibiotics, whereas YcbB in combination with elevated (p)ppGpp rendered the bulk of the population resistant only to β-lactams that did not inactivate the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB (Table 5).
evidence: This is established knowledge contrasted with the findings of this study.

claim: YcbB in combination with elevated (p)ppGpp rendered the bulk of the population resistant only to β-lactams that did not inactivate the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB.
source: Persistence emerges from stochastic events that render a limited number of bacterial cells transiently tolerant to multiple families of antibiotics, whereas YcbB in combination with elevated (p)ppGpp rendered the bulk of the population resistant only to β-lactams that did not inactivate the L,D-transpeptidase activity of YcbB (Table 5).
evidence: This is based on MIC determinations shown in Table 5.

claim: Plasmids pKT2(ycbB) and pKT8(relA 1–455) conferred ampicillin and ceftriaxone resistance to mutants from the Keio collection deficient in production of the Lon protease and the polyphosphate kinase PPK.
source: In addition, plasmids pKT2(ycbB) and pKT8(relA 1–455) conferred ampicillin and ceftriaxone resistance to mutants from the Keio collection deficient in production of the Lon protease and the polyphosphate kinase PPK (data not shown) indicating that tolerance and resistance do not involve the same (p)ppGpp-regulated circuits.
evidence: This is based on experimental data (not shown).

claim: Tolerance and resistance do not involve the same (p)ppGpp-regulated circuits.
source: In addition, plasmids pKT2(ycbB) and pKT8(relA 1–455) conferred ampicillin and ceftriaxone resistance to mutants from the Keio collection deficient in production of the Lon protease and the polyphosphate kinase PPK (data not shown) indicating that tolerance and resistance do not involve the same (p)ppGpp-regulated circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that resistance occurred in Lon and PPK mutants.
